tier_reason: Issue #3 (camel-cdr, 2020-12-19) posts ns-per-sample tables for float and double that include cpp11random (std::normal_distribution with std::minstd_rand, per the benchmark's src/cpp11random.cpp and readme); every number in claimed_speedup matches. First-party numbers with no CPU model, compiler or flags, so C.

corrections.caveats: First-party claim in a GitHub issue comment with no CPU model, compiler or flags, so tier C. The std::normal_distribution baseline is driven by std::minstd_rand, not std::mt19937 (confirmed in the benchmark's src/cpp11random.cpp), and the standard library implementation is not stated; the ziggurat uses a cheap LCG, so the gap partly reflects RNG cost (the benchmark's null entry is 1.049 ns float, 1.149 ns double). In the same tables the benchmark's clt4 entry (sum of 4 uniforms, an approximation) runs at 4.064 ns float and 4.088 ns double, essentially tied with ziggurat_new. The code in the issue is the author's proposed template, not literally the current cauldron function: random.h's dist_normal(f)_zig is described as based on Doornik's implementation with a single lookup table, and in the current random.h the float version defaults to 128 blocks while the double version defaults to 256 blocks (DIST_NORMAL_ZIG_COUNT), so the link is by author and design, not identical code. The double version builds a 64-bit value from two 32-bit LCG outputs per the issue. The cauldron repo has tools/random/bench.c (referenced from random.h) but publishes no results. Issue dated 2020-12-19; last repo commit 2025-02-01. The lead's '4.0 ns versus 7.3-7.8 ns' compares against the benchmark's existing ziggurat, while the std::normal_distribution figures are 8.852 ns and 17.009 ns.

notes: All numbers verified on the issue page; license MIT, 143 stars, last commit 2025-02-01 ('small changes') confirmed, so stale is right. Only the caveats were extended (clt4 tie, 256-block double default in current random.h).

tier_reason: The ROOT blog post (author Jonas Hahnfeld, ROOT developer) gives 30 ns initial, about 9 ns tuned, 62 ns for TRandom1, about 3 ns for TRandom3 and 8 ns for Sibidanov's assembly, on one core of an AMD Ryzen 9 3900 with GCC 8.3.1; the benchmark code (rootbench root/math/mathcore/TRandomBenchmarks.cxx, BM_Rndm over TRandom1, TRandom3, TRandomMixMax, TRandomRanluxpp) is public, but optimisation flags are not stated and the measured code predates the June 2021 correctness changes, so first-party C, not A.

corrections.caveats: The benchmark compares against TRandom1 (original RANLUX) and does not beat std::mt19937, PCG or xoshiro: in the same post TRandom3 (Mersenne Twister) is about 3 ns per number, about 3x faster. TRandom1 yields only 24-bit single-precision numbers while RANLUX++ yields 48-52 bits per double, so the work per number differs. The post itself notes that Luescher's newer RANLUX (ranlxd) was measured at 30 ns for double values in a cited review, so against modern RANLUX the tuned 9 ns is about 3.3x faster (derived from page data), not 6.9x; std::ranlux24/std::ranlux48 from <random> were not measured. The measured code predates correctness changes in June 2021 (commits '[mathcore] Ensure full modulo operation in mod_m', 'RANLUX++: Convert LCG state to RANLUX numbers', 'RANLUX++: Extract only 48 bits per number', per the RanluxppEngineImpl.cxx history page; the blog says 52 bits per double), so the 9 ns figure was not re-measured for the shipped implementation and the tier is capped at C. Optimisation flags are not stated; the benchmark source is public (root-project/rootbench PR #200, merged 2020-12-15, root/math/mathcore/TRandomBenchmarks.cxx) but no results are checked in. The last commit shown for RanluxppEngineImpl.cxx was 2021-06-23 (the June 2021 commit 'Move RANLUX++ implementation to directory' split helpers into a subdirectory not covered by that file history); last_commit above is the overall ROOT repo (large project, judged only for math/mathcore RanluxppEngine*).

notes: Every number in claimed_speedup and the hardware/compiler fields match the raw blog markdown; ROOT license LGPL v2.1+, 3.3k stars and newest commit 2026-10-02 confirmed. Added the post's own caveat that Luescher's newer RANLUX runs at 30 ns per double, which shrinks the derived gain to about 3.3x.
